newsitem.title: USA: U.S. T-bonds rally, soft data ease rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. T-bonds rally, soft data ease rate hike fears.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended higher on Tuesday as soft retail sales and bargain hunting helped offset fears of a short-term interest rate hike later this month, traders and analysts said.

"Again and again, we see bargain hunters show up above 7.0 percent (30-year bond yield). Some people definitely think there is value there, and there surely is if (interest) rates remain steady," one trader said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended up 23/32 at 96-06/32 to yield 7.06 percent.

Bonds started the session on a weak note, pressured by a newspaper report hinting at a possible 50-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate later this month. The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on September 24.
The article quoted unnamed Fed officials in the wake of the Jackson Hole, Wyo., annual conference hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.

The report was particularly negative for the front end since market players had only priced in a moderate 25-point increase in the 5.25-percent funds rate. As a result, the 2-year note/30-year bond yield curve flattened to 75 points.
A minor negative for the Treasury market was concern over a U.S. missile strike on Northern Iraq and an ensuing spike in oil prices.
But traders said they did not expect any long-term impact on the credit market as the United States is highly unlikely to embark on a major military operation in the Gulf.
"Rising oil prices make you shy," said MCM MoneyWatch senior economist Astrid Adolfson, commenting on the one commodity whose gains have the broadest inflationary impact.
"This shows that (President Bill) Clinton can address a military threat," she added.
But combined fears of higher interest rates and rising oil prices forced the 30-year bond yield to a session high of 7.18 percent -- a level that attracted bargain hunters.

"Today was all short-covering. People sold aggressively ahead of the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) report. It came as expected and nobody wanted to sell which accounts for a large move in a market with little volume," Adolfson noted.
The NAPM report -- regarded by many as the month's second most-important data after the payrolls -- edged up in August, but not to lofty, inflationary levels.
In the absence of aggressive selling above the 7.0-percent bond yield, the market found comfort in an afternoon report about soft August retail sales.

The Lynch, Jones and Ryan's Redbook retail sales index rose 0.8 percent in August, not enough to offset a steep July decline -- and not a particularly buoyant read on the American consumer's mood in the back-to-school shopping season.

"Everybody is now waiting for the payrolls," said Adolfson, echoing the prevailing market sentiment. "It's the pattern we have seen in recent months. The market moves on the payrolls and then trade back and forth in-between reports."

The August job report is due out on Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. A Reuter survey puts payrolls at up 244,000 vs. up 193,000 in July, and average hourly earnings at up 0.3 percent vs down 0.2 percent in July.
The new three-month Treasury bill closed unchanged at a 5.18-percent rate, so did the one-year bill, at 5.59 percent. The new six-month bill shed one point to 5.35 percent.

The two-year note closed up 2/32 at 99-21/32 to yield 6.31 percent, the five-year note up 6/32 at 99-7/32 and 6.69 percent, and the 10-year note up 13/32 at 100-25/32 and 6.89 percent. -- 212-859-1666
